title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 257
paragraphs: Now all who have a temple set up to the Theban Zeus, or who belong to the district of Thebes, sacrifice goats and abstain from sheep — for not all Egyptians equally reverence the same gods, except only Isis and Osiris (whom they say is Dionysus); these they all reverence alike. But those who have a temple of Mendes or belong to the Mendesian district abstain from goats and sacrifice sheep. The men of Thebes, and those who after their example abstain from sheep, say this custom was established among them for the following reason. Heracles (they say) had an earnest desire to see Zeus, and Zeus did not desire to be seen by him; at last, when Heracles was insistent in entreaty, Zeus devised this trick — he flayed a ram and held in front of him the head of the ram that he had cut off, and he put on over himself the fleece, and then showed himself to Heracles. Hence the Egyptians make the image of Zeus with the face of a ram; and the Ammonians do so also after their example, being settlers from both the Egyptians and the Ethiopians, and using a language that is a mixture of both tongues. And in my opinion it is from this god that the Ammonians took the name they bear, for the Egyptians call Zeus Amun. The Thebans, then, do not sacrifice rams but hold them sacred for this reason. Yet on one day of the year, at the feast of Zeus, they cut up and flay a single ram in the same manner, and cover the image of Zeus with its skin, and then they bring up to it another image of Heracles. When this is done, all who are in the temple beat themselves in lamentation for the ram, and then they bury it in a sacred tomb.
